common_name: Red Tiger Sikkim Banana (Maroon-Mottled Darjeeling Banana)

planting.note: Set out rhizome divisions or potted offsets once frost danger has passed, in deep, humus-rich soil that stays evenly moist; 'Red Tiger' is a selection of the cold-hardy Sikkim banana chosen for the heavy maroon-red mottling on its leaf undersides and pseudostem, which is more consistent and pronounced than on the straight species.

directions: 'Red Tiger' is a named selection of Musa sikkimensis grown for the dramatic wine-red blotching and streaking that covers its leaf undersides, midribs, and pseudostem far more heavily than on typical seed-grown Sikkim bananas. Give it rich, well-drained but moisture-retentive soil and dappled to partial sun, since the huge paddle leaves scorch and tear in hot, dry, windy sites. Like its parent species it is one of the hardier ornamental bananas, tolerating winters into zone 7 if the rhizome is covered with a thick layer of mulch or straw after the pseudostem is cut back following the first hard freeze. Feed heavily through the growing season and divide congested clumps every few years to keep the coloration vivid on fresh growth.

planting.note: Set out divisions or container-grown pups once nights stay reliably warm, in rich, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; Thai Black is grown mainly as a foliage and stem-color accent, valued for its near-black pseudostem and dark purple-black leaf midribs rather than for its seedy fruit.

directions: Thai Black stands out among ornamental bananas for its dark, near-black pseudostem and leaf midribs, which read as deep aubergine to black against the plant's green blades and make it a striking specimen or backdrop plant in a tropical-look border. It wants the same rich, steadily moist, well-drained soil and heavy feeding that other fast-growing ornamental Musa need to reach full size in a single season. Full sun brings out the darkest stem color, though a little afternoon shade is tolerated in hot climates. It has no more cold tolerance than most acuminata- and balbisiana-type ornamentals, so gardeners outside the warmest zones should plan to dig and overwinter the rhizome indoors or grow it in a large container that can be moved under cover before frost.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions or potted offsets in spring once the soil has warmed, in rich, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to partial shade; this hardy hybrid banana, raised in the UK from cold-tolerant Himalayan and Southeast Asian Musa parentage, is grown by cold-climate banana enthusiasts as a hardier, better-looking alternative to Musa basjoo.

directions: Helen's Hybrid is a cold-hardy banana raised by an amateur breeder in the United Kingdom from cold-tolerant Musa parentage and has since become a favorite among hardy-banana collectors as a step up from Musa basjoo, combining similar or slightly better cold tolerance with broader leaves and better-proportioned pseudostems. Grow it in deep, humus-rich, evenly moist soil, since like other large-leaved bananas it wilts quickly if it dries out. In hard-freeze climates the pseudostem is killed back each winter, but the rhizome survives reliably with a heavy mulch of straw or leaves piled over the crown after the first freeze; in milder zones the trunk itself can persist and the plant reaches a much greater height. Feed generously through the growing season to support the rapid, lush growth this hybrid is known for.

planting.note: Plant divisions or potted offsets once frost danger has passed, in rich, well-drained soil that stays consistently moist; this Yunnan species is grown as a flowering ornamental banana closely related to Musa itinerans and Musa laterita, valued for its upright, felted yellow-orange floral bracts and comparatively good cold tolerance for its size.

directions: Musa flaviflora is a lesser-grown flowering banana from the mountains of Yunnan, China, closely related to the walking banana (Musa itinerans) and grown mostly by specialist and botanic garden collections for its upright clusters of felty, yellow to burnt-orange floral bracts, which are showier and longer-lasting than the foliage. It comes from higher, cooler elevations than most ornamental Musa species and shows correspondingly better cold tolerance, tolerating brief dips into the mid-teens Fahrenheit with the rhizome protected by heavy mulch. Give it deep, humus-rich soil with reliable moisture and some shelter from strong wind, which tatters the broad leaves. Where winters exceed its tolerance, cut back the frost-killed pseudostem and mulch heavily over the crown to allow regrowth from the rhizome the following spring.
